full_prose_under_review.title: What Massachusetts Pharmacists and Pharmacy Interns May Administer: Authority, Conditions and Practice Requirements
full_prose_under_review.topic: Pharmacist administration / Authority, eligible medications, conditions of administration and practice requirements
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The three pharmacist routes in the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 definition of Administer and the pharmacist's limited place on the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) practitioner list; the age limit and conditions of 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), which sits among the exemptions from the requirement to register; the eligible-medication list and its legal bases, the conditions for dispensing by administration and prescriber reassessment, the route, dose and packaging conditions, and the training, CPR, competency, emergency, counseling, record-keeping, adverse-event and privacy requirements of Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124, with who reports an improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event under 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D, which such events are reportable and within what period; the administration notation and prescriber communication; administration by order in a registered opioid treatment program under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e), with the federal limits in 21 CFR 1306.07(a) and (d) on narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment; immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6); and the boundary to vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order under 105 CMR 700.003(F)
learning_objectives: Name the three routes by which the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 definition of Administer reaches a registered pharmacist, and state what gates each one.
Explain why M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) does not place a pharmacist on the same footing as a physician, and identify its possession limb as well as its administration limb.
State what 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) authorizes, for which drugs and which persons, where it sits in the regulation, and the four conditions it attaches.
Apply the circular's conditions for dispensing by administration, including the registration point, the age of the person treated, the valid prescription and prescriber reassessment.

Decide whether a medication is eligible under Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124, and keep the regulation's mental health and substance use disorder reach apart from the statute's testosterone, sexually transmitted infection and HIV prevention routes.
Apply the subcutaneous-or-intramuscular route limit, the manufacturer labeling and REMS requirement, and the single-dose packaging and prescribing condition, including the effect of refills.
State the training, CPR, competency, emergency-readiness, counseling and privacy requirements a pharmacist or pharmacy intern must meet to administer, and the information the pharmacy must maintain.

Sort adverse events into those that should be communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours and those that must be reported immediately, and, beside the circular's statement that the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting to the Board, state who reports an improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event under Board regulations and the statute, which such events are reportable and within what period, and what the circular's sentence leaves open about who carries the responsibility and which events it covers.
Distinguish what the circular asks of prescribers and pharmacists about the administration notation and administration records from a condition of administering.

Recognise that a pharmacist's administration of medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order is confined to a registered opioid treatment program, and keep that route apart from the listed long-acting injectables for substance use disorders, and state the federal limit on prescribing a Schedule II narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment.

State what 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) authorizes a registered pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer, to whom and on what conditions, and recognise 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) and 105 CMR 700.003(F) as further administration authorities, so that the circular's eligible list is not taken for the whole of what a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may administer.
Separate what the statute, the regulation and the Department's circular each say, including which of them names a pharmacy intern, and weigh the force of the words each one uses.

orientation.text: No single provision tells a Massachusetts pharmacist what she may administer. For most medications the answer is assembled from four texts that do different work. The definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 names the registered pharmacist and sets out three routes through which a pharmacist's direct application of a controlled substance to the body of a patient counts as administering. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) lists the practitioners who may possess and administer controlled substances, and includes the pharmacist only as limited by two further provisions. The Department's regulation at 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) and the Department's Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 of 11 March 2026 then carry the working pathway: which medications a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may administer on a prescription, to whom, on what conditions, by what route and in what dose and packaging, with what training, counseling, records and reporting, and what the prescription should say. The circular describes itself as Department guidance, and the difference between guidance, regulation and statute matters when its verbs are read. The pathway is not a general licence to administer any prescription injectable. It reaches the medications on an exhaustive list, for a pharmacist or pharmacy intern who meets the conditions attached to it. Nor is the pathway the whole of the authority to administer: the same regulation separately authorizes immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) and administration by order in an opioid treatment program under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e), and 105 CMR 700.003(F) provides for vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order, all taken up later in this section.

The statutory definition does the first sorting. Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 means the direct application of a controlled substance, whether by injection, inhalation, ingestion or any other means, to the body of a patient or research subject by one of the persons the definition lists. Clause (b) covers a nurse at the direction of a practitioner in the course of his professional practice. Clause (c) covers a registered pharmacist acting in accordance with one of three things, and each is gated differently. Under the first, the pharmacist acts in accordance with regulations promulgated by the Department, in consultation with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Department of Mental Health, governing pharmacist administration of medications for treatment of mental health and substance use disorder, and at the direction of a prescribing practitioner in the course of the practitioner's professional practice: two gates, a regulation and a direction. Under the second, the pharmacist acts in accordance with a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care in the course of the practitioner's professional practice. Under the third, the pharmacist acts in accordance with a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections, including those defined in regulation by the Department under section 121B of chapter 111, or for the prevention of HIV. The statute writes the regulation gate and the practitioner's direction into the first route only; the second and third routes are gated on a prescription, so a condition drawn from the mental health and substance use disorder route is not carried across to testosterone, to sexually transmitted infections or to HIV prevention by the statute itself.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) is a different kind of provision. It lists practitioners who, when acting in accordance with applicable federal law and any provision of chapter 94C which is consistent with federal law, in good faith, and in the course of a professional practice for the alleviation of pain and suffering or for the treatment or alleviation of disease, may possess controlled substances as may reasonably be required for the purpose of patient treatment, and may administer controlled substances or cause them to be administered under the practitioner's direction by a nurse. The list closes with the words 'or veterinarian when registered under said section 7'. A physician appears on it without any limiting phrase. The pharmacist appears as 'pharmacist as limited by said subsection (g) of said section 7 and section 24B1/2 of said chapter 112', that is, by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g) and by M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2, the collaborative practice provision taught in the collaborative-practice sections. Two consequences follow. The sentence carries a possession limb, measured by what patient treatment reasonably requires, as well as an administration limb. And a pharmacist cannot read s. 9(a) as a freestanding grant equal to a physician's, because the pharmacist's place on the list runs through those two provisions. Section 9(a) is not the whole of a pharmacist's administration authority either: the definition of Administer and the Department's regulation and guidance are separate sources, each with its own conditions.

The working pathway turns on a list. Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 states that the generic medications it lists, which may have multiple brand names, are the only medications eligible to be administered by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern. The list has five categories: long-acting injectable antipsychotics (aripiprazole, aripiprazole lauroxil, fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate, risperidone and risperidone ER); long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders (buprenorphine and naltrexone); gender-affirming care medications (testosterone, all salts); HIV prevention medications (cabotegravir, and lenacapavir or other medications to prevent HIV); and sexually transmitted infection medications (ceftriaxone as an IM injection, and doxycycline or other medications to treat chlamydia). Three features of the list decide most questions. It is stated by generic name, so a brand the list does not mention is not excluded for that reason. It is closed rather than illustrative, so a long-acting injectable that is not named does not come in because it shares a class with one that is; whatever reaches beyond a single named generic is written into the entries themselves, in testosterone's all salts and in the two entries that extend to other medications to prevent HIV and other medications to treat chlamydia. And testosterone sits in the list as a gender-affirming care medication, matching the statute's route for a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, so the purpose of the prescription, not the molecule, places it in the category. Eligibility is not obligation: the circular states that there is no requirement for pharmacists or pharmacy interns to administer these medications. Read with its Purpose, which ties the circular to 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), the list closes the pathway the circular describes; it is not read as taking away the separate authorities the regulation grants elsewhere, such as immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6).

The regulation sits between the statute and the list. 105 CMR 700.004(B) is headed Exemptions from Requirement to Register, and paragraph (9) within it authorizes a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern to dispense by administration FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs to persons 18 years of age or older, provided that: (a) the pharmacist or pharmacy intern is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112; (b) the administration is conducted pursuant to a valid prescription; (c) the prescription is subject to reassessment at appropriate intervals as determined by the prescriber; and (d) the activity is conducted in accordance with guidelines adopted by the Department. Condition (d) is where the regulation hands the detail to the Department: the guidelines shall include, but not be limited to, requirements for the specific drugs permitted, accredited training, current CPR certification, continued competency, pre-administration patient counseling, dosing and administration only in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling, administration of medication including controlled substances as necessary for the management of medical emergencies, record keeping, and reporting of adverse events. The regulation's own words reach mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs, the subject of the statute's first route; the gender-affirming care, HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection categories line up instead with the statute's second and third routes, and the circular lists all five categories together. Kept apart, each proposition stays with its source: the routes and their gates come from the statute, the regulation supplies the age limit, the conditions and the required contents of the guidelines for mental health and substance use disorder drugs, and the list and its detailed requirements come from Department guidance. Two points about actors follow. Clause (c) of the statutory definition names only a registered pharmacist, and the regulation names a pharmacy intern in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) only for FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs. For testosterone, HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection medications, the text that names a pharmacy intern is the Department's circular, which does so in its Purpose, in its conditions for dispensing by administration and in the heading of its list.

The circular states its own conditions for every medication on its list. A pharmacist or a pharmacy intern may, without obtaining a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration (MCSR), dispense by administration FDA-approved drugs on the eligible list to persons 18 years or older, provided that: (a) the pharmacist or pharmacy intern is authorized to dispense controlled substances, in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112; (b) administration is conducted pursuant to a valid prescription; (c) administration is not intravenous; (d) the medication is available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills; (e) the prescription is subject to reassessment by the prescriber at appropriate intervals, as determined by the prescriber, if applicable; and (f) the activity is conducted in accordance with Department guidelines. Two of these are easily misread. Not needing an MCSR does not remove condition (a), so the pharmacist or intern still has to be authorized to dispense controlled substances under chapter 112. And reassessment belongs to the prescriber: under the circular's Prescriber Assessment section, prescribers must regularly re-assess the patient and prescription at appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, to be determined by the prescriber; that assessment does not preclude valid prescriptions with available refills; and a pharmacist or intern who has questions about the interval between assessments is encouraged, but not required, to communicate with the prescriber before administering. The circular's age condition covers all five categories, while the regulation states its age limit for mental health and substance use disorder drugs and the statute's second and third routes state none; the course that is safe on any reading is to administer under the pathway only to persons 18 years or older.

Once a medication is on the list, the circular controls how it is given. A pharmacist or pharmacy intern may only administer an eligible medication by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any risk evaluation and mitigation (REMS) requirements for the specific medication administered. The regulation points the same way on labeling: under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d)6. the Department's guidelines shall include requirements for dosing and administration of the medications only in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling. Conditions (c) and (d) of dispensing by administration are easily merged and should be kept apart. Condition (c) is that administration is not intravenous, however well trained the pharmacist. Condition (d) has two parts: the medication is available in single-dose packaging, and it is prescribed in single doses, with or without refills. The first part concerns the packaging and the second the prescription, and the closing words mean that a prescription for a single dose may carry refills without failing the condition. The statute gates its second and third routes on a prescription alone, while the circular states its route, dose and packaging conditions for every medication on its list, testosterone and the HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection medications included; the course that is safe on any reading is to meet both.

The circular then attaches requirements to the person who administers. To administer, a pharmacist or pharmacy intern must first receive training that is accredited by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Council on Pharmaceutical Education or a similar health authority or professional body appropriate for the medications being administered and their respective patient populations, and the training shall include learning modules on techniques for administration by injection. The pharmacist or intern must maintain current certification in cardiopulmonary resuscitation, must maintain continued competency regarding the populations served, medications administered and current guidelines, and must maintain competency in management of medical emergencies that may arise as a result of administration of eligible medications. Continuing education programs are, in the circular's words, one way to maintain competency; the continuing education requirement itself is covered in the section on continuing education. Before administering a dose of an approved medication, the pharmacist or intern must provide customary patient counseling, which may include information about common side-effects, drug interactions, dietary requirements, injection site reaction and other information routinely provided to patients upon dispensing, as appropriate within the professional judgment of the pharmacist and in accordance with 247 CMR 2.00 et seq. At all times during the course of dispensing and administration, the pharmacist or intern must maintain the privacy and confidentiality of the patient, in accordance with 247 CMR 2.00 et seq. and 42 CFR Part 2 as applicable. These requirements are written as must and shall; what is left to judgment is the content of the counseling, not whether it is given.

Two further requirements concern the record and what follows when something goes wrong, and their force differs. A pharmacy where any of the eligible medications are administered must maintain patient consent; patient screening information, including at least date of birth and other relevant vital statistics, known allergies, and other medications taken; the type of medication administered; the manufacturer; the lot number; the expiration date; the date of administration; the route and site of administration; the pharmacist or pharmacy intern, by signature or initials and title; any adverse outcome; and any adverse event. The duty sits on the pharmacy, and the circular's Record Keeping section states no retention period. Adverse events run on two tiers. Any adverse event or reaction occurring as a result of the administration should be appropriately communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours. If the event includes death, a life-threatening outcome, inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, additional treatment, testing or monitoring in a hospital or emergency department, or a persistent or significant incapacity or substantial disruption of the ability to conduct normal life functions, it must be immediately reported to the prescriber, and an adverse event must also be immediately reported where emergency medical services are required. Reporting to the prescriber does not end the matter. The circular adds that if the adverse event is the result of a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event, the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, in accordance with Board regulations. That sentence is Department guidance, and the Board regulations it points to say who files, which events they require to be reported and by when. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the pharmacy's Manager of Record reports to the Board any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing. Under 247 CMR 20.02(2) the Manager of Record reports a serious adverse drug event that occurs as a result of a patient's interaction with a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, within seven business days of the knowledge of the event by any pharmacy employee. The statute places the corresponding duties on the pharmacy and its manager of record: under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health of improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing, and under s. 39D(c) the manager of record reports such a serious adverse drug event to the same three recipients, with the report to the Board due within 7 business days of any pharmacy employee's knowledge of it. Neither the rule nor the statute names the pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered as the one who files. The texts leave two points open, both in the circular's sentence. The first is who carries the responsibility: the circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board, while the rule and the statute give the filing to the Manager of Record and the pharmacy and do not say what that continuing responsibility consists of. The second is which events the sentence covers. An event that is neither an improper dispensing resulting in serious injury or death nor a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy is not one that 247 CMR 20.02 or M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D requires to be reported: a dispensing error that causes only a minor reaction, for example, or a serious adverse drug event, with no improper dispensing, from a listed medication that was not manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. Both of those events are ones the circular's sentence names, because on its face it names every dispensing error and every serious adverse drug event. Its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' may narrow that set to the events the Board regulations require to be reported, or may govern only how the report is made; 247 CMR 20.01 provides that all reports required by 247 CMR 20.00 shall be made in the manner and format determined by the Board. The texts do not settle which reading is right. The safe course covers both points. The pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered makes sure the event reaches the Manager of Record at once, rather than assuming either that the Manager of Record's duty leaves them with nothing to do or that they must file in the Manager of Record's place; a report is made to the Board for any event the circular names, even where 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D would not require one; and the reports those texts do require are made within their periods. Any adverse event still goes to the prescriber on the circular's tiers, and the rest of Board reporting is covered in the section on quality-related events and the reports they trigger.

The prescription and the prescriber relationship are addressed in the circular's section on pharmacist-prescriber communication, and every sentence in it is written as a recommendation or an encouragement rather than as a condition. Prescribers issuing prescriptions for eligible medications, and pharmacists or pharmacy interns administering them, are strongly encouraged to engage in regular communication to ensure patient safety, continued patient progress, medication adherence and emergency management. Prescribers should make clear that they intend an eligible medication to be administered by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern by including the notation 'for pharmacist administration' on the prescription. A pharmacist or pharmacy intern who receives a prescription for an eligible medication without the notation is encouraged to contact the prescriber if, in their professional judgment, it appears the medication is intended to be administered, rather than dispensed to the patient for administration outside the pharmacy. Pharmacists and pharmacy interns are strongly encouraged to send administration records to prescribers as soon after administration as practical, which is a different thing from the adverse-event communication and reports above. Prescribers are urged to issue a separate prescription for appropriate emergency medication, as needed, and prescribers and pharmacists are encouraged to develop an emergency medication protocol. Nothing in the section makes a missing notation invalidate a prescription, contact with the prescriber is not stated as a precondition of administering, and 'as soon after administration as practical' is not a fixed clock.

One route sits outside the prescription pathway altogether. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) provides that a pharmacist is authorized to administer controlled substances in an Opioid Treatment Program pursuant to an order and in accordance with guidance issued by the Department. The circular's note to its conditions for dispensing by administration puts the point more sharply: a pharmacist may administer medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order, only in a registered opioid treatment program. Both the setting and the instrument differ from the ordinary pathway. The setting is a registered opioid treatment program, so the route is not available in a pharmacy that is not one, and the instrument is an order, so a valid prescription does not open the route. Methadone is not on the eligible list, and it is the note rather than the list that addresses a pharmacist's administration of methadone for addiction treatment. Read alone, the note's 'only' might seem to confine every administration of an addiction-treatment medication to such a program, but that reading cannot stand with the rest of the circular, whose Purpose and list authorize a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer long-acting injectable buprenorphine and naltrexone under its prescription conditions; since the note itself speaks of administration pursuant to an order, it is read as governing that kind of administration. On that reading methadone, which is not on the list, is administered by a pharmacist only pursuant to an order in a registered opioid treatment program, while the listed long-acting injectables may be administered in a pharmacy on a prescription that meets the circular's conditions, so the two routes for addiction treatment should not be merged into one. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) and the note both name a pharmacist; neither names a pharmacy intern for this route, so an intern should not treat it as available. Federal law adds a parallel limit for methadone: under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a narcotic drug in Schedule II, such as methadone, for maintenance or detoxification treatment, if separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program; paragraph (b) separately lets a practitioner who is not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs to initiate maintenance or detoxification treatment, not more than a three-day supply at one time while arrangements are made for referral, without renewal or extension, and paragraph (c) imposes no limitation on a physician or authorized hospital staff administering or dispensing narcotic drugs in a hospital as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to persons with intractable pain; neither (b) nor (c) provides for prescribing, while 1306.07(d), the paragraph that includes prescribing, reaches Schedule III, IV and V narcotic drugs.

The pathway has edges, and neighbouring authorities are easily confused with it. The eligible list names no vaccine, but that does not close vaccines to pharmacists. Under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), which sits among the same exemptions from the requirement to register, a registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other immunizations designated by the Department to persons five years of age or older, provided that the person is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112 or Department guidance; the administration is conducted pursuant to the order of a practitioner; each pharmacy that provides immunizations follows Department guidelines to disclose whether it receives vaccines free of charge through the Massachusetts Immunization Program and notifies patients that there may be a difference in cost between immunization services provided at a pharmacy and at a primary care provider's office; and the activity is conducted in accordance with guidelines adopted by the Department. Those guidelines shall include requirements for accredited training, pre-administration education and screening, vaccine storage and handling, administration of medication, including controlled substances as necessary for the management of medical emergencies, information on primary care providers in the pharmacy's area where the person is younger than 18, counseling on the importance of a relationship with a pediatric or family practice where the visit is for a childhood immunization other than influenza vaccine, record keeping, and reporting of adverse events. The age floor there is five years, not the 18 years of paragraph (9), and the instrument is a practitioner's order rather than a prescription for a listed medication. Separately, 105 CMR 700.003(F) lets a health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department, or a student duly enrolled in an approved or accredited program for licensure as a health care professional and acting in accordance with the policies of that program, possess and administer any vaccine designated by the Commissioner for the prevention of a pandemic, novel, or other vaccine-preventable disease, provided the Commissioner determines that there are or will be insufficient health care professionals available for timely vaccine administration and issues an order authorizing such administration, with administration in accordance with that order and the order or prescription of a duly registered practitioner. That authority, with its student conditions, training and protocols, is covered in the section on dispensing and administering without an individual prescription, as is dispensing under the statewide standing orders. Vaccine administration derived from a collaborative practice agreement belongs to the collaborative-practice sections. Paragraph (6) also names a pharmacy technician; what a pharmacy technician may do is a separate subject, covered in the section on pharmacy technicians.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist in a Massachusetts community pharmacy receives a valid prescription for testosterone cypionate for gender-affirming care for a 26-year-old patient, written for a single dose with five refills, for a product supplied in single-dose packaging, and carrying no administration notation. The pharmacist is authorized to dispense controlled substances, completed accredited training that included injection-technique modules, and holds current CPR certification. The patient asks to have the dose given at the pharmacy. A colleague objects on three grounds: no Department regulation stands behind this route, the refills defeat the single-dose condition, and a prescription without the notation cannot be used for administration. The colleague adds that the dose could at least be given intravenously, since the pharmacist is well trained.
steps: Place the medication. Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 lists testosterone, all salts, as a gender-affirming care medication, and this prescription is for gender-affirming care, so testosterone cypionate on this prescription is an eligible medication.

Answer the first objection from the statute. The definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 gates the testosterone route on a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care; the statute writes the regulation gate into the mental health and substance use disorder route and does not carry it across.

Run the circular's conditions for dispensing by administration. No MCSR needs to be obtained, the pharmacist is authorized to dispense controlled substances under chapter 112, the patient is 18 or older, the prescription is valid, and prescriber reassessment at appropriate intervals does not preclude refills.

Answer the second objection from condition (d), which requires that the medication be available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills. A single dose with five refills, in single-dose packaging, satisfies it.

Answer the third objection from the communication section. Prescribers should include the notation 'for pharmacist administration', and a pharmacist receiving a prescription without it is encouraged to contact the prescriber where it appears the medication is intended to be administered. Contact is a sensible step here, but neither sentence is written as a condition of administering or as making the prescription invalid.

Reject the intravenous suggestion. A pharmacist or pharmacy intern may only administer an eligible medication by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements, and condition (c) is that administration is not intravenous, whatever the pharmacist's training.

Check the requirements on the person administering. The accredited training and current CPR certification are in place, and the pharmacist must also maintain continued competency and competency in management of medical emergencies; customary patient counseling has to come before the dose.

Close out the administration: the pharmacy must maintain the circular's administration record, and the pharmacist is strongly encouraged to send the administration record to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical.
worked_examples.resolution: None of the colleague's three objections is a reason to refuse, and the intravenous suggestion is excluded outright. After customary counseling the dose may be given by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection in accordance with the labeling, provided the pharmacist also maintains the competencies the circular requires, and the pharmacy then maintains the administration record. The error the scenario invites is carrying the regulation gate from the mental health and substance use disorder route into the testosterone route, and reading guidance that says should or encouraged as a rule of validity.

worked_examples.scenario: A 35-year-old patient who receives care from a registered opioid treatment program brings two documents to a community pharmacy that is not an opioid treatment program: a valid prescription for an extended-release naltrexone injection, and a prescription written for methadone for maintenance treatment of the patient's opioid addiction. The patient asks the pharmacist to administer both on site. The pharmacist once worked at an opioid treatment program, where he administered methadone from orders, and reasons that a prescription is at least as strong an instrument as an order.
steps: Start with the list. Methadone is not among the generic medications Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 lists as eligible, so the ordinary pathway does not reach it.

Find where methadone is addressed. The circular's note provides that a pharmacist may administer medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order, only in a registered opioid treatment program, and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) authorizes a pharmacist to administer controlled substances in an Opioid Treatment Program pursuant to an order and in accordance with Department guidance.

Apply both elements. This pharmacy is not a registered opioid treatment program, and the instrument presented is a prescription rather than an order. The note states the setting with 'only', so neither the methadone prescription nor the pharmacist's past work in a programme opens the route here.

Add the federal layer, which points the same way. Methadone is a Schedule II narcotic drug, and under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a Schedule II narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment, if separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program; paragraph (b) separately lets a practitioner who is not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs to initiate maintenance or detoxification treatment, not more than a three-day supply at one time while arrangements are made for referral, without renewal or extension, and paragraph (c) imposes no limitation on a physician or authorized hospital staff administering or dispensing narcotic drugs in a hospital as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to persons with intractable pain. Neither of those paragraphs includes prescribing; the paragraph that includes prescribing for that purpose, 1306.07(d), is confined to Schedule III, IV and V narcotic drugs. Federal law therefore provides no route for the methadone prescription either.

Turn to the naltrexone. Naltrexone is listed among the long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders, so the extended-release injection is an eligible medication on a prescription through the ordinary pathway.

Apply the ordinary conditions to it: a patient 18 years or older, a valid prescription, a pharmacist authorized to dispense controlled substances under chapter 112, subcutaneous or intramuscular injection only in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements, and a medication available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills.

Keep eligibility and obligation apart. The circular states there is no requirement for pharmacists or pharmacy interns to administer these medications, so giving the naltrexone is the pharmacist's choice.
worked_examples.resolution: The methadone may not be administered at this pharmacy under either Massachusetts route taught here, and federal law provides no route for a methadone prescription for maintenance treatment; the naltrexone injection is eligible on the ordinary conditions if the pharmacist chooses to give it. The error the scenario invites is treating a prescription as a substitute for an order in a registered opioid treatment program, and treating every medication for addiction treatment as travelling the same pathway.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist working in a clinic reads M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) and concludes that, because pharmacists are named in the same sentence as physicians, she may keep a supply of a controlled substance for treating clinic patients and have a nurse administer doses under her direction, exactly as the clinic's physicians do. She has no collaborative practice agreement and relies on no authority other than s. 9(a).
steps: Read what the sentence grants. A listed practitioner may possess controlled substances as may reasonably be required for the purpose of patient treatment, and may administer controlled substances or cause them to be administered under the practitioner's direction by a nurse; there is a possession limb and an administration limb.

Read the conditions stated for the listed practitioners: acting in accordance with applicable federal law and any provision of chapter 94C consistent with federal law, in good faith, and in the course of a professional practice for the alleviation of pain and suffering or for the treatment or alleviation of disease.

Read the two entries that matter. A physician is listed without a limiting phrase. The pharmacist is listed 'as limited by said subsection (g) of said section 7 and section 24B1/2 of said chapter 112'.

Apply the limiting phrase. Her place on the list runs through M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2, and she relies on neither, so the sentence does not give her the freestanding authority it gives the physicians, whether for keeping a supply or for administering or directing a nurse.

Do not overcorrect. Section 9(a) is not the whole of a pharmacist's administration authority; the definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 reaches a registered pharmacist through its own three routes, each with its own gate.
worked_examples.resolution: Section 9(a) standing alone does not put her on the physicians' footing, either for the supply or for administration. The error the scenario invites is reading a shared list as conferring identical authority, and stopping before the words 'as limited by' that qualify the pharmacist's entry.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy manager wants to expand the pharmacy's administration service with three additions: a long-acting injectable antipsychotic whose generic name is not on the Department's list, on the reasoning that the list samples the class; ceftriaxone given intravenously because a prescriber prefers that route; and cabotegravir for HIV prevention supplied under a brand name the list does not mention. She also tells the staff pharmacists that once the service is advertised each of them must administer any eligible medication a patient requests, because the circular authorizes it.
steps: Test the unlisted antipsychotic. Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 states that the generic medications it lists are the only medications eligible to be administered by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern, and the antipsychotic category is a named list, so an unlisted long-acting injectable does not come in by class.

Test the ceftriaxone. It is listed, as an IM injection, but a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may only administer an eligible medication by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, and condition (c) is that administration is not intravenous; a prescriber's preference does not change the route limit.

Test the brand-name cabotegravir. The list is stated by generic name and the circular notes that the listed generic medications may have multiple brand names, so the brand's absence from the list does not exclude it; it still has to be given by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection in accordance with its labeling and any REMS requirements.

Test the staffing instruction against the circular, which states there is no requirement for pharmacists or pharmacy interns to administer these medications; what the circular authorizes is not a duty to administer on request.

Keep the authority in proportion. The pathway reaches the medications on an exhaustive list; it is not a general licence to administer every prescription injectable, and advertising a service does not widen it.
worked_examples.resolution: Of the three additions only the brand-name cabotegravir survives, and then only if it is given by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection; the unlisted antipsychotic fails on the closed list, the intravenous ceftriaxone fails on the route limit, and the circular gives no support for treating eligibility as a duty to administer. The error the scenario invites is treating the list as illustrative, treating a listed medication as open to any route, and confusing what the circular permits with what it requires.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy intern who has completed accredited training and holds current CPR certification administers an eligible long-acting injectable antipsychotic by intramuscular injection to a 40-year-old patient on a valid prescription. Within minutes the patient has a severe reaction, the pharmacist calls emergency medical services, and the patient, seriously injured by the reaction, is admitted to hospital overnight. The next morning the pharmacist learns that the product drawn up was not the product prescribed. The intern proposes to note the reaction in the pharmacy's system and fax the prescriber at the end of the day, reasoning that the circular allows 24 hours. The pharmacist adds that, because the intern gave the injection, the intern must file the report with the Board.
steps: Start with the general tier. Any adverse event or reaction occurring as a result of administration should be appropriately communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours.

Check for the immediate tier. Emergency medical services were required, and the event led to inpatient hospitalization; either fact means the adverse event must be immediately reported to the prescriber, so an end-of-day fax is too late.

Add the Board, and identify who files. The wrong product was administered, so the adverse event is the result of a dispensing error, and the circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, in accordance with Board regulations. Those regulations place the filing with the pharmacy's Manager of Record: under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the Manager of Record reports to the Board an improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing, and this improper dispensing seriously injured the patient. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) the pharmacy also informs the Department of Public Health, as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing. Reporting to the prescriber discharges neither. The texts do not say what the intern's continuing responsibility under the circular consists of, so the pharmacist is not simply wrong to see a responsibility in the intern, but the rule does not make the intern the filer in the Manager of Record's place. The safe course is for the intern and the pharmacist to bring the event to the Manager of Record at once and to make sure the Board report is made within seven business days and the Department is informed in time.

Make the record. The pharmacy where the medication was administered must maintain, among the other items, the type of medication administered, its manufacturer, lot number and expiration date, the date, route and site of administration, the intern's signature or initials and title, and the adverse outcome and adverse event.

Keep the emergency requirement in view. To administer, a pharmacist or pharmacy intern must maintain competency in management of medical emergencies that may arise as a result of administration, alongside the current CPR certification the intern already holds.
worked_examples.resolution: The reaction had to be reported to the prescriber immediately, not within 24 hours. Because the improper dispensing resulted in serious injury, the pharmacy's Manager of Record reports it to the Board within seven business days under 247 CMR 20.02(1), and the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b). The circular says the intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board in accordance with Board regulations, and the texts leave open what that responsibility consists of; the intern's safe course is to see that the event reaches the Manager of Record at once and that the required reports are made in time. The pharmacy's record has to capture the adverse event and its outcome. The errors the scenario invites are treating the 24-hour communication as the outer limit for every adverse event, treating a report to the prescriber as the end of the reporting, and settling the intern's position either way beyond what the texts say: neither assuming the intern files in the Manager of Record's place nor assuming the intern has no part in seeing the report made.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist who holds no individual Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration, but is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, is presented with a valid prescription for an extended-release naltrexone injection for a 17-year-old patient. The prescription was issued five months ago for a single dose with refills, and the pharmacist has not heard from the prescriber since. A colleague says the missing registration and the age of the prescription are the problems to solve.
steps: Take the registration point first. The circular lets a pharmacist or pharmacy intern dispense by administration without obtaining a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration, provided the pharmacist or intern is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, which this pharmacist is.
Place the medication. Naltrexone is listed among the long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders.

Now the person treated. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) authorizes dispensing by administration of FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs to persons 18 years of age or older, and the circular's conditions likewise speak of persons 18 years or older; a 17-year-old is outside both.

Deal with reassessment. The prescription is subject to reassessment by the prescriber at appropriate intervals determined by the prescriber; the circular gives quarterly as an example, says reassessment does not preclude valid prescriptions with available refills, and treats routine communication about the interval as encouraged, but not required, before administration.
Conclude on the pathway's own terms. The age of the person treated, not the registration or the refills, is what closes the pathway for this patient.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist may not administer the injection to the 17-year-old under this pathway. The absence of an MCSR is not an obstacle, and the five-month-old prescription with refills raises at most a question about reassessment that the pharmacist is encouraged, not required, to take up with the prescriber. The error the scenario invites is concentrating on registration and refills and missing the age of the person treated.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 reaches a registered pharmacist through ______ routes. Name the gate on each.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Three. The mental health and substance use disorder route is gated on Department regulations and the direction of a prescribing practitioner; the testosterone route on a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care; the third route on a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or for the prevention of HIV.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: under the statute, a pharmacist administering under a prescription for treatment of a sexually transmitted infection must also satisfy the regulation gate written into the mental health and substance use disorder route.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The statute writes the regulation gate into the first route only; the sexually transmitted infection route is gated on a prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which clause of the definition of Administer covers a nurse, and what does it require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Clause (b): a nurse at the direction of a practitioner in the course of his professional practice. The pharmacist routes are in clause (c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What two things does M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) let a listed practitioner do, and how is the first measured?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Possess controlled substances as may reasonably be required for the purpose of patient treatment, and administer controlled substances or cause them to be administered under the practitioner's direction by a nurse. The possession limb is measured by what patient treatment reasonably requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) the pharmacist appears 'as limited by' which two provisions?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Subsection (g) of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7, and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), which drugs may a pharmacist or pharmacy intern dispense by administration, and to whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs, to persons 18 years of age or older, on the conditions the paragraph sets.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four conditions lettered (a) to (d) in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9).
retrieval_prompts.answer: (a) Authorization to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112; (b) administration pursuant to a valid prescription; (c) a prescription subject to reassessment at appropriate intervals as determined by the prescriber; (d) conduct in accordance with guidelines adopted by the Department, which shall include requirements for nine listed subjects.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under which heading of 105 CMR 700.004 does paragraph (9) appear?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 700.004(B), headed Exemptions from Requirement to Register.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: For which categories on the eligible list is a pharmacy intern named in the Department's circular but not in the statute or 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Testosterone for gender-affirming care, HIV prevention medications and sexually transmitted infection medications. Clause (c) of the statutory definition of Administer names only a registered pharmacist, and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) names a pharmacy intern only for FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does a pharmacist need a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration to administer an eligible medication under the circular?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. The circular says a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may dispense by administration without obtaining an MCSR, but condition (a) still requires authorization to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a prescription that carries refills cannot be used for administration because the prescriber has to reassess the patient.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Prescribers must regularly re-assess at appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, to be determined by the prescriber, but the circular says this does not preclude valid prescriptions with available refills.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist has questions about the interval since the prescriber last reassessed the patient. Must she contact the prescriber before administering?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Routine communication with the prescriber about the interval between assessments is encouraged, but not required, prior to administration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because the Department's list gives examples, any long-acting injectable antipsychotic may be administered by a pharmacist.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The circular states the listed generic medications are the only medications eligible, so an unlisted long-acting injectable antipsychotic is outside the list.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the two long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders on the eligible list.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Buprenorphine and naltrexone.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two entries on the eligible list reach other medications for a stated purpose?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Lenacapavir, which extends to other medications to prevent HIV, and doxycycline, which extends to other medications to treat chlamydia.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is a testosterone prescription for a purpose other than gender-affirming care within the listed category?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Testosterone, in all salts, is listed as a gender-affirming care medication, and the statute's route is a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care; the purpose of the prescription places it in the category.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: By what routes may a pharmacist or pharmacy intern administer an eligible medication, and what must the administration follow?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements for the specific medication administered.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescription for an eligible injectable is written for one dose with three refills. Does it meet condition (d)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes, provided the medication is also available in single-dose packaging. Condition (d) requires single-dose packaging and prescribing in single doses, with or without refills.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What training must a pharmacist or pharmacy intern receive before administering under the circular?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Training accredited by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Council on Pharmaceutical Education or a similar health authority or professional body appropriate for the medications and patient populations, including learning modules on techniques for administration by injection.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: completing continuing education programs is the only way to maintain the competency the circular requires.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The circular calls continuing education programs one way to maintain competency regarding the populations served, medications administered and current guidelines.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When must counseling be given, and what may it include?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Customary patient counseling must be provided prior to administering a dose of an approved medication. It may include common side-effects, drug interactions, dietary requirements, injection site reaction and other information routinely provided upon dispensing, as appropriate within the pharmacist's professional judgment.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who must maintain the administration record, and what does it contain?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy where the eligible medication is administered. It contains patient consent; screening information including at least date of birth and other relevant vital statistics, known allergies and other medications taken; type of medication; manufacturer; lot number; expiration date; date of administration; route and site; the pharmacist or intern's signature or initials and title; and any adverse outcome and adverse event.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: An adverse reaction follows administration, with no listed serious outcome and no need for emergency medical services. What does the circular say?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It should be appropriately communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which adverse events must be reported immediately rather than communicated within 24 hours?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An event with death; a life-threatening outcome; inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization; additional treatment, testing or monitoring in a hospital or emergency department; or a persistent or significant incapacity or substantial disruption of the ability to conduct normal life functions, which must be immediately reported to the prescriber. An adverse event where emergency medical services are required must also be immediately reported, as the adverse-event section outlines.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: once an adverse event caused by a dispensing error has been reported to the prescriber, no report to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy can be required.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board, in accordance with Board regulations, and under 247 CMR 20.02(1) the pharmacy's Manager of Record reports to the Board an improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to it. A dispensing error that results in no serious injury or death is not required to be reported under that paragraph, but the circular's sentence still names it, and the texts do not settle whether a report to the Board is then called for; the safe course is to bring it to the Manager of Record at once and report it to the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D, who reports an improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event that follows administration, and which such events are reportable?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 247 CMR 20.02 the pharmacy's Manager of Record reports an improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death to the Board, and a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, each within seven business days. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health of improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death, and under s. 39D(c) the manager of record reports such a serious adverse drug event. Neither text names the pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered as the one who files, although the circular says that person remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board in accordance with Board regulations; the texts do not say what that responsibility consists of, and the safe course is for that person to make sure the event reaches the Manager of Record at once and that the required reports are made in time. The circular's sentence also names dispensing errors and serious adverse drug events that these texts do not reach, and the texts do not settle whether its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' limit it to the events they reach, so the safe course is to report those events to the Board as well.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A serious adverse drug event follows administration of a commercially manufactured long-acting injectable that the pharmacy did not compound, and there was no dispensing error. Is a report to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy called for?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 20.02(2) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(c) do not require one, because they reach a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. The circular's sentence, on its face, names every serious adverse drug event, and the texts do not settle whether its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' limit it to the events those provisions reach or govern only how the report is made. The safe course is for the pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered to bring the event to the Manager of Record at once and for a report to be made to the Board. Separately, if a listed serious outcome occurred or emergency medical services were required, the event must be reported to the prescriber immediately.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: For how long, and under what standards, must patient privacy be maintained?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At all times during the course of dispensing and administration, in accordance with 247 CMR 2.00 et seq. and 42 CFR Part 2 as applicable.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What notation does the circular ask prescribers to put on a prescription meant for pharmacist administration, and how strongly does it ask?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'for pharmacist administration'. Prescribers should include it; the circular does not write it as a condition of administering.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescription for an eligible medication arrives without the notation, and it appears the medication is intended to be administered. What does the circular say about contacting the prescriber?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist or pharmacy intern is encouraged to contact the prescriber. Contact is encouraged rather than stated as a precondition, and the circular does not say the missing notation invalidates the prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When should administration records go to the prescriber, and is the timing a mandate?
retrieval_prompts.answer: As soon after administration as practical. Pharmacists and pharmacy interns are strongly encouraged to send them; the circular sets no fixed deadline.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where, and on what instrument, may a pharmacist administer methadone for addiction treatment?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pursuant to an order, and only in a registered opioid treatment program, under the circular's note and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does 21 CFR 1306.07 provide for a practitioner to prescribe methadone for maintenance or detoxification treatment?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No paragraph of 1306.07 provides for it. Paragraph (a) lets a practitioner separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a Schedule II narcotic drug such as methadone for that purpose, and paragraph (d), which includes prescribing, is confined to Schedule III, IV and V narcotic drugs.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist who may administer a listed medication has to do so when a patient presents a prescription for it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The circular states there is no requirement for pharmacists or pharmacy interns to administer these medications.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is the Department's prescription pathway a general licence to administer any prescription injectable, and does its eligible list mark the outer edge of what a Massachusetts pharmacist or pharmacy intern may administer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No on both counts. The pathway reaches the medications on the circular's exhaustive list, for a pharmacist or pharmacy intern who meets its conditions, but it is not the only authority to administer. Under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) a registered pharmacist or pharmacy intern may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other Department-designated immunizations to persons five years of age or older, pursuant to the order of a practitioner and on that paragraph's conditions; under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) a pharmacist may administer controlled substances in an Opioid Treatment Program pursuant to an order; and under 105 CMR 700.003(F) a health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department may possess and administer a Commissioner-designated vaccine once the Commissioner has made the insufficiency determination and issued an authorizing order, in accordance with that order and a practitioner's order or prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), who may dispense by administration which immunizations, to whom, and on what instrument?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other immunizations designated by the Department, to persons five years of age or older, pursuant to the order of a practitioner and on the paragraph's other conditions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a pharmacy that provides immunizations disclose and tell patients under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6)(c)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It shall follow Department guidelines to disclose whether it receives vaccines free of charge through the Massachusetts Immunization Program, and shall notify patients that there may be a difference in cost between immunization services provided at a pharmacy and at a primary care provider's office.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist is asked to give influenza vaccine to a seven-year-old on a practitioner's order. Do the circular's 18-or-older condition and its eligible list stop her?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Those belong to the circular's prescription pathway. Immunization rests on 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), which reaches influenza vaccine for persons five years of age or older pursuant to the order of a practitioner, provided she is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112 or Department guidance, the pharmacy makes the required disclosure and cost notice, and the activity follows the Department's guidelines, which must include providing information on primary care providers in the pharmacy's geographic area for a person younger than 18.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 105 CMR 700.003(F) authorize, and where is it taught?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department, or a student duly enrolled in an approved or accredited program for licensure as a health care professional and acting in accordance with its policies, may possess and administer a vaccine designated by the Commissioner for the prevention of a pandemic, novel, or other vaccine-preventable disease, provided the Commissioner determines that there are or will be insufficient health care professionals available for timely vaccine administration and issues an authorizing order; administration must accord with that order and a duly registered practitioner's order or prescription. It is covered in the section on dispensing and administering without an individual prescription.

quick_review.text: Clause (c) of the definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 reaches a registered pharmacist through three routes: Department regulations plus a prescribing practitioner's direction for mental health and substance use disorder medications, a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, and a prescription for treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or prevention of HIV.
Only the first statutory route carries a regulation gate and a direction gate; the second and third are gated on a prescription.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) lets listed practitioners possess controlled substances as reasonably required for patient treatment and administer them, or cause them to be administered under the practitioner's direction by a nurse.
The pharmacist is on the s. 9(a) list only as limited by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2, so the sentence does not give a pharmacist a physician's freestanding authority.

105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), under the heading Exemptions from Requirement to Register, authorizes a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to dispense by administration FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs to persons 18 years of age or older.

Its conditions are authorization to dispense controlled substances under M.G.L. c. 112, a valid prescription, prescriber reassessment at appropriate intervals, and conduct in accordance with Department guidelines that shall include requirements for nine listed subjects.

Under the circular, a pharmacist or intern may administer without obtaining an MCSR, to persons 18 years or older, pursuant to a valid prescription subject to prescriber reassessment, and in accordance with Department guidelines.

Prescribers must regularly re-assess at appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, determined by the prescriber; refills remain possible, and communication about the interval is encouraged but not required before administration.

Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 lists by generic name the only medications eligible for administration by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern under its prescription pathway, in five categories: long-acting injectable antipsychotics, long-acting injectables for substance use disorders, testosterone for gender-affirming care, HIV prevention medications and sexually transmitted infection medications.

The eligible list closes the circular's prescription pathway only: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) separately authorizes immunizations, 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) administration by order in an Opioid Treatment Program, and 105 CMR 700.003(F) vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order.
Testosterone is eligible in all salts, and two entries reach further than a named generic: lenacapavir or other medications to prevent HIV, and doxycycline or other medications to treat chlamydia.
There is no requirement for a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer any eligible medication.

An eligible medication is administered only by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements, and administration is not intravenous.
The conditions for dispensing by administration include that the medication is available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills.

To administer, a pharmacist or intern must first receive accredited training with injection-technique modules, and must maintain current CPR certification, continued competency and competency in management of medical emergencies.
Customary patient counseling must be provided before a dose of an approved medication is administered; its content is left to what is appropriate in the pharmacist's professional judgment.

The pharmacy where eligible medications are administered must maintain a record of consent, screening information, the medication, manufacturer, lot number, expiration date, date, route and site, the administering pharmacist or intern, and any adverse outcome or event.
Adverse events should be communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours, and must be reported immediately where a listed serious outcome occurs or emergency medical services are required.

The circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting to the Board an adverse event that results from a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event, in accordance with Board regulations; under 247 CMR 20.02 the pharmacy's Manager of Record files, and that rule requires a report only for improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death or for a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, each within seven business days. The circular's sentence names every dispensing error and serious adverse drug event, and the texts settle neither what the administering pharmacist's or intern's responsibility consists of nor whether the sentence reaches events the rule does not; the safe course is to bring the event to the Manager of Record at once and report to the Board any event the circular names.
Privacy and confidentiality must be maintained at all times during dispensing and administration, in accordance with 247 CMR 2.00 et seq. and 42 CFR Part 2 as applicable.
Prescribers should add the notation 'for pharmacist administration'; without it, a pharmacist who judges the medication is intended for administration is encouraged to contact the prescriber.
Pharmacists and pharmacy interns are strongly encouraged to send administration records to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical.

A pharmacist may administer medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order only in a registered opioid treatment program; the long-acting injectable buprenorphine and naltrexone on the eligible list are administered on a prescription under the circular's conditions.

Under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) a registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other Department-designated immunizations to persons five years of age or older, pursuant to the order of a practitioner and on the paragraph's conditions, including the pharmacy's disclosure and cost notice and Department guidelines.

105 CMR 700.003(F) separately provides for a Commissioner-designated vaccine to be possessed and administered once the Commissioner makes the insufficiency determination and issues an order, in accordance with that order and a practitioner's order or prescription.

Clause (c) of the definition of Administer names only a registered pharmacist, and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) names a pharmacy intern only for mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs; for the other listed categories the pharmacy intern is named in the circular.

Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a Schedule II narcotic drug such as methadone for maintenance or detoxification treatment; 1306.07(b) lets a practitioner without that registration dispense, but not prescribe, not more than a three-day supply at one time while arranging referral, 1306.07(c) imposes no limitation on hospital use as an incidental adjunct to treatment of conditions other than addiction or on treating intractable pain, and 1306.07(d) allows prescribing only for Schedule III, IV and V narcotic drugs.

decision_logic.condition: The request is to administer a medication for addiction treatment, such as methadone, pursuant to an order.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the setting is a registered opioid treatment program. If it is, a pharmacist may administer pursuant to the order and in accordance with Department guidance; if it is not, the route is closed. A pharmacy intern should not rely on this route, which the texts state for a pharmacist.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription is presented for a medication to be administered at the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Check the eligible list by generic name. A medication that is not listed, and is not within the entries for other medications to prevent HIV or other medications to treat chlamydia, is not eligible under the circular's pathway, whatever its class or the pharmacist's skill.
Confirm the prescription is for gender-affirming care; both the listed category and the statutory route turn on that purpose.

decision_logic.condition: The medication is eligible and the patient wants it administered.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the person treated is 18 years or older, the prescription is valid, and the pharmacist or intern is authorized to dispense controlled substances under M.G.L. c. 112; no MCSR needs to be obtained.

decision_logic.condition: Someone insists that a Department regulation must stand behind testosterone, HIV prevention or sexually transmitted infection administration.
decision_logic.action: Point to the statute: the regulation gate is written into the mental health and substance use disorder route only, and the other two routes are gated on a prescription. Then apply the circular's conditions, which it states for every listed medication.
