decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist has questions about how recently the prescriber reassessed the patient.
decision_logic.action: Treat the reassessment interval as the prescriber's to determine; communicating with the prescriber about it is encouraged but not required before administering, and reassessment does not rule out refills.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist or intern is preparing to administer.
decision_logic.action: Confirm accredited training that included injection-technique modules has been received, CPR certification is current, and continued competency and competency in management of medical emergencies are maintained.

decision_logic.condition: The medication is eligible and the question is how to give it.
decision_logic.action: Use subcutaneous or intramuscular injection only, following manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements for that medication, and do not administer intravenously.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is checked against the dose and packaging condition.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the medication is available in single-dose packaging and is prescribed in single doses; refills do not defeat the condition.

decision_logic.condition: The dose is ready to be given.
decision_logic.action: Provide customary patient counseling first, and keep the patient's privacy and confidentiality throughout dispensing and administration.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription has no administration notation.
decision_logic.action: If, in professional judgment, it appears the medication is intended to be administered rather than dispensed for administration outside the pharmacy, contact the prescriber as the circular encourages; the circular does not make the notation or the contact a condition of administering.

decision_logic.condition: An eligible medication has been administered.
decision_logic.action: Make sure the pharmacy's record captures the items the circular lists, and send the administration record to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical, as the circular strongly encourages.

If it involves a listed serious outcome, report it to the prescriber immediately, and if emergency medical services were required, report it immediately as the adverse-event section outlines; otherwise communicate it to the prescriber within 24 hours.

decision_logic.condition: The adverse event is the result of a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event.
decision_logic.action: Read the circular's statement that the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board, in accordance with Board regulations, with 247 CMR 20.02. If an improper dispensing resulted in serious injury or death, the pharmacy's Manager of Record reports it to the Board within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to it, and under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing. If a serious adverse drug event arose from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, the Manager of Record reports it to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction within seven business days of any pharmacy employee's knowledge of it. If neither applies, 247 CMR 20.02 and s. 39D require no report, but the circular's sentence still names the event, and the texts do not settle whether its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' limit the events it covers or govern only how the report is made. In every case the pharmacist or pharmacy intern who administered makes sure the event reaches the Manager of Record at once, a report is made to the Board for any dispensing error or serious adverse drug event, and the reports 247 CMR 20.02 and s. 39D require are made within their periods. Board reporting is covered in full in the section on quality-related events and the reports they trigger.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist is asked to administer an eligible medication and does not wish to.
decision_logic.action: Treat eligibility as permission, not duty; the circular states there is no requirement to administer these medications.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist relies on M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) alone to possess or administer a controlled substance.
decision_logic.action: Read the pharmacist's entry, which is limited by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2. Relying on neither, the pharmacist does not stand on a physician's footing under s. 9(a); look to the definition of Administer and the Department's regulation and guidance instead.

Leave the eligible list aside, since it names no vaccine, and identify the authority. Influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine or another Department-designated immunization for a person five years of age or older on a practitioner's order comes under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), with its conditions on authorization to dispense controlled substances, the pharmacy's disclosure and cost notice, and Department guidelines. A vaccine designated by the Commissioner and administered under an order issued on the Commissioner's insufficiency determination comes under 105 CMR 700.003(F), covered in the section on dispensing and administering without an individual prescription, and vaccine administration under a collaborative practice agreement is taken up in the collaborative-practice sections.

decision_logic.condition: Someone treats the circular's eligible list as the whole of what a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may administer.
decision_logic.action: Correct the premise. The list closes the circular's prescription pathway, but 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) separately authorizes immunization, 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) authorizes a pharmacist to administer controlled substances in an Opioid Treatment Program pursuant to an order, and 105 CMR 700.003(F) provides for vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order.

ma_vs_federal.text: Federal law adds its own limit where methadone is used for addiction treatment. Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a narcotic drug in Schedule II, such as methadone, to a narcotic dependent person for maintenance or detoxification treatment, if separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program and in compliance with DEA regulations regarding treatment qualifications, security, records and unsupervised use of the drugs; paragraph (b) separately lets a practitioner who is not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs to initiate maintenance or detoxification treatment, not more than a three-day supply at one time while arrangements are made for referral, without renewal or extension, and paragraph (c) imposes no limitation on a physician or authorized hospital staff administering or dispensing narcotic drugs in a hospital as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to persons with intractable pain; under 1306.07(d) a practitioner may administer or dispense, including prescribe, a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for that use. Both that federal limit and the Massachusetts order-only route in a registered opioid treatment program bind a Massachusetts pharmacist, and where both reach the act the stricter governs. The federal rules on narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment are covered in full in the section on special controlled substance prescription rules and narcotic treatment limits.

exceptions.text: Refills are permitted: a prescription in single doses may carry refills without failing condition (d), and prescriber reassessment does not preclude valid prescriptions with available refills.

Testosterone is listed in all salts, and two entries reach beyond a named generic for a stated purpose: lenacapavir or other medications to prevent HIV, and doxycycline or other medications to treat chlamydia.
Methadone is not on the eligible list, but a pharmacist may administer medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order in a registered opioid treatment program.
Eligibility creates no duty: there is no requirement for a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer any listed medication.

No Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration needs to be obtained to dispense by administration under the circular, although the pharmacist or intern must be authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112.
Routine communication with the prescriber about the interval between reassessments is encouraged, but not required, before administration.

The circular does not describe a prescription without the administration notation as unusable; it encourages contact with the prescriber where it appears the medication is intended to be administered.

An adverse event with a listed serious outcome falls outside the 24-hour communication tier and must be reported to the prescriber immediately, and an adverse event requiring emergency medical services must also be reported immediately.

Not every dispensing error or serious adverse drug event after administration is one that 247 CMR 20.02 requires to be reported to the Board: 247 CMR 20.02(1) reaches improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death, and 247 CMR 20.02(2) a serious adverse drug event arising from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. That is not an exception to the circular's sentence on reporting to the Board, which on its face names every dispensing error and every serious adverse drug event; the texts do not settle whether its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' narrow that set or govern only the manner of reporting, so the safe course for an event outside 247 CMR 20.02 is still to bring it to the Manager of Record at once and report it to the Board.

The statute's regulation gate and practitioner-direction gate belong to the mental health and substance use disorder route only; the testosterone route and the sexually transmitted infection or HIV prevention route rest on a prescription.

The circular's 18-or-older condition and eligible list do not govern immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), which reaches influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other Department-designated immunizations for persons five years of age or older, pursuant to the order of a practitioner.

timing_deadlines.event: Training accredited as the circular requires, including injection-technique modules
timing_deadlines.consequence: A pharmacist or pharmacy intern must first receive it in order to administer.
A pharmacist or pharmacy intern must maintain current certification in cardiopulmonary resuscitation in order to administer.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Prior to administering a dose of an approved medication
timing_deadlines.consequence: Required of the pharmacist or pharmacy intern; its content is left to what is appropriate within the pharmacist's professional judgment.

timing_deadlines.event: Prescriber reassessment of the patient and prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, to be determined by the prescriber
timing_deadlines.consequence: Prescribers must regularly re-assess; the assessment does not preclude valid prescriptions with available refills.

timing_deadlines.event: Adverse event or reaction resulting from administration of a listed medication
timing_deadlines.consequence: Should be appropriately communicated to the prescriber.

timing_deadlines.event: Adverse event with a listed serious outcome
timing_deadlines.consequence: Must be reported to the prescriber.

timing_deadlines.event: Adverse event where emergency medical services are required
timing_deadlines.consequence: Must be reported, as the circular's adverse-event section outlines.

timing_deadlines.event: Report of improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to the improper dispensing, under 247 CMR 20.02(1); under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b), as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy's Manager of Record reports to the Board under the rule, and the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health under the statute; a report to the prescriber under the circular does not stand in for either.

timing_deadlines.event: Report of a serious adverse drug event arising from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven business days of the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy's Manager of Record reports to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, under 247 CMR 20.02(2) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(c).

timing_deadlines.event: Sending the administration record to the prescriber
timing_deadlines.timeframe: As soon after administration as practical
timing_deadlines.consequence: Strongly encouraged by the circular; it is not written as a fixed deadline or as a condition of the administration.

timing_deadlines.event: Contacting the prescriber about a missing administration notation
timing_deadlines.consequence: Encouraged where, in professional judgment, it appears the medication is intended to be administered; it is not stated as a precondition of administering.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: No retention period is stated in the circular's Record Keeping section
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy must maintain the listed information; that section does not fix how long.

forms_records.text: A pharmacy where any of the eligible medications are administered must maintain: patient consent; patient screening information, including at least date of birth and other relevant vital statistics, known allergies, and other medications taken; type of medication administered; manufacturer; lot number; expiration date; date of administration; route and site of administration; pharmacist or pharmacy intern (signature or initials and title); adverse outcome, if any; and adverse event, if any.

The prescription for an eligible medication should carry the notation 'for pharmacist administration', which is how the circular asks prescribers to show that they intend administration by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern.
Administration is conducted pursuant to a valid prescription, subject to reassessment by the prescriber at appropriate intervals, as determined by the prescriber, if applicable.
The prescription is written in single doses, with or without refills, for a medication available in single-dose packaging.

For the statute's second route the instrument is a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, and for the third a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or for the prevention of HIV.

The statute's first route runs on regulations promulgated by the Department, in consultation with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Department of Mental Health, together with the direction of a prescribing practitioner.
105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d) requires the Department's guidelines to include, but not be limited to, requirements for nine subjects, among them record keeping and reporting of adverse events.
In a registered opioid treatment program the instrument for administering medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, is an order, not a prescription.
Pharmacists and pharmacy interns are strongly encouraged to send administration records to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical.

Where an adverse event is the result of a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event, the circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, in accordance with Board regulations. Under 247 CMR 20.02 the report is made by the pharmacy's Manager of Record: to the Board for improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, and to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction for a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, each within seven business days. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) the pharmacy also informs the Department of Public Health of such improper dispensing. Under 247 CMR 20.01, all reports required by 247 CMR 20.00 are made in the manner and format determined by the Board. The circular's sentence names every dispensing error and every serious adverse drug event, and the texts do not settle whether it reaches events that 247 CMR 20.02 does not; the safe course is to bring any such event to the Manager of Record at once and make a report to the Board.

Manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements for the specific medication govern how an eligible medication is administered, and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d)6. requires the Department's guidelines to include requirements for dosing and administration only in accordance with that labeling.

Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 is the Department document that lists the eligible medications by generic name. For its two categories of long-acting injectable antipsychotics and long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders, the list names the specific drugs permitted to be administered pursuant to 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9), a subject on which 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d)1. requires the Department's guidelines to include requirements. The opening words of 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) reach FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs, so the list's gender-affirming care, HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection categories fall outside those words and line up instead with clauses (c)(ii) and (c)(iii) of the definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1.

Prescribers are urged to issue separate prescriptions for appropriate emergency medications, as needed, alongside prescriptions for medications to be administered by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern, and prescribers and pharmacists are encouraged to develop an emergency medication protocol.

Immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) is conducted pursuant to the order of a practitioner, and the Department's guidelines for it shall include requirements for record keeping and reporting of adverse events.

role_duties.role: Registered pharmacist under the definition of Administer
role_duties.duty: Act in accordance with one of the three routes in clause (c) of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1: Department regulations plus a prescribing practitioner's direction for mental health and substance use disorder medications, a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, or a prescription for treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or prevention of HIV.

role_duties.role: Department of Public Health
role_duties.duty: Promulgate the regulations governing pharmacist administration of mental health and substance use disorder medications in consultation with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Department of Mental Health, and adopt guidelines that include requirements for the specific drugs permitted, training, CPR certification, continued competency, pre-administration counseling, dosing and administration only in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling, administration for medical emergencies, record keeping and reporting of adverse events.

role_duties.role: Prescribing practitioner
role_duties.duty: Give the direction the mental health and substance use disorder route requires, and issue the prescription on which the testosterone route and the sexually transmitted infection or HIV prevention route rest.

role_duties.role: Prescriber of an eligible medication
role_duties.duty: Regularly re-assess the patient and prescription at appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, that the prescriber determines, and make clear an intent for pharmacist administration with the notation 'for pharmacist administration', which the circular says prescribers should do.

role_duties.role: Prescriber and administering pharmacist or pharmacy intern
role_duties.duty: Engage in regular communication to ensure patient safety, continued patient progress, medication adherence and emergency management, as the circular strongly encourages; prescribers are urged to issue separate prescriptions for appropriate emergency medications, and prescribers and pharmacists are encouraged to develop an emergency medication protocol.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern administering an eligible medication
role_duties.duty: Administer under the circular's pathway only listed generic medications, to persons 18 years or older, pursuant to a valid prescription, while authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, only by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection in accordance with manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements, not intravenously, and only where the medication is available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern preparing to administer
role_duties.duty: First receive accredited training that includes injection-technique modules, keep CPR certification current, maintain continued competency and competency in management of medical emergencies, and provide customary patient counseling before the dose.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern throughout dispensing and administration
role_duties.duty: Maintain the privacy and confidentiality of the patient at all times, in accordance with 247 CMR 2.00 et seq. and 42 CFR Part 2 as applicable.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy where eligible medications are administered
role_duties.duty: Maintain the circular's list of information: patient consent, screening information, medication type, manufacturer, lot number, expiration date, date, route and site of administration, the administering pharmacist or intern, and any adverse outcome and adverse event.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern after an adverse event
role_duties.duty: Communicate it to the prescriber within 24 hours, as the circular says should be done, or report it immediately where a listed serious outcome occurs or emergency medical services are required. Where the event is the result of a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event, the circular says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting it to the Board, in accordance with Board regulations, which give the filing to the Manager of Record; the texts do not define that continuing responsibility, and the safe course is to bring the event to the Manager of Record at once and make sure that a report to the Board is made for any dispensing error or serious adverse drug event the circular names, including one that 247 CMR 20.02 and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D do not reach, and that the reports those texts require are made within their periods; the texts do not settle whether the circular's words 'in accordance with Board regulations' limit the events it covers.

role_duties.role: Manager of Record of the pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Report to the Board an improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of the serious injury or death related to it, under 247 CMR 20.02(1); and report a serious adverse drug event arising from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy to the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction, within seven business days of any pharmacy employee's knowledge of it, under 247 CMR 20.02(2) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(c).

role_duties.role: Pharmacy, after an improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death
role_duties.duty: Inform the Department of Public Health as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing, under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern receiving a prescription without the notation
role_duties.duty: Contact the prescriber, as the circular encourages, where professional judgment suggests the medication is intended to be administered rather than dispensed for administration outside the pharmacy.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern after administration
role_duties.duty: Send the administration record to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical, as the circular strongly encourages.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist or pharmacy intern asked to administer
role_duties.duty: Decide whether to administer; the circular states there is no requirement to administer the eligible medications.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist in a registered opioid treatment program
role_duties.duty: Administer medications for addiction treatment, including methadone, pursuant to an order and in accordance with guidance issued by the Department.

role_duties.role: Registered pharmacist or pharmacy intern giving immunizations under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6)
role_duties.duty: Administer influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine or other immunizations designated by the Department only to persons five years of age or older, pursuant to the order of a practitioner, while authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112 or Department guidance, and in accordance with the Department's guidelines.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy that provides immunizations
role_duties.duty: Follow Department guidelines to disclose whether it receives vaccines free of charge through the Massachusetts Immunization Program, and notify patients that there may be a difference in cost between immunization services provided at a pharmacy and at a primary care provider's office.

role_duties.role: Physician on the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) list
role_duties.duty: Possess and administer controlled substances, or cause them to be administered by a nurse under the physician's direction, on the conditions the sentence states, with no limiting phrase attached to the entry.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist on the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) list
role_duties.duty: Treat the possession and administration authority in s. 9(a) as limited by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 rather than as a freestanding grant.

role_duties.role: Nurse
role_duties.duty: Administer at the direction of a practitioner in the course of his professional practice under clause (b) of the definition of Administer, and administer controlled substances that a practitioner listed in s. 9(a) causes to be administered under that practitioner's direction.

common_traps.text: Treating the eligible list as examples of a class. The circular states the listed generic medications are the only medications eligible.
Rejecting a medication because its brand name is not on the list. The list is by generic name and the listed medications may have multiple brand names.
Treating testosterone as eligible whatever the purpose of the prescription. Both the listed category and the statutory route are for gender-affirming care.

Carrying the regulation gate and the practitioner-direction gate from the mental health and substance use disorder route into the testosterone, sexually transmitted infection or HIV prevention routes, which the statute gates on a prescription.
Treating clause (b) of the definition of Administer, which covers a nurse at the direction of a practitioner, as the pharmacist's route. The pharmacist routes are in clause (c).
Reading the pharmacist into M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(a) on a physician's footing, or overlooking that the sentence carries a possession limb measured by what patient treatment reasonably requires.
Assuming s. 9(a) is the whole of a pharmacist's administration authority, or, in the opposite direction, that its limiting phrase leaves the pharmacist with no administration authority anywhere.

Reading 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) as reaching testosterone, HIV prevention or sexually transmitted infection medications. Its words reach FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs.

Reading the statute or 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) as naming a pharmacy intern for testosterone, HIV prevention or sexually transmitted infection medications. Clause (c) names only a registered pharmacist, the regulation names an intern only for mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs, and the intern is named for the other categories in the circular.
Assuming that administering without an MCSR removes the need to be authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112.
Overlooking the age of the person treated. The regulation speaks of persons 18 years of age or older and the circular of persons 18 years or older.
Treating quarterly as a fixed reassessment deadline, reassessment as ruling out refills, or contact with the prescriber about the interval as required before administering.
Treating injection training as opening any route. Administration is by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection only, and not intravenous.

Assuming refills disqualify a single-dose prescription, or reading condition (d) as concerned with packaging alone. It requires single-dose packaging and single-dose prescribing, with or without refills.
Stopping once the route is right and overlooking manufacturer approved labeling and any REMS requirements for the specific medication.

Treating any injection course as sufficient, or a lapsed CPR certification as enough. The training must be accredited as the circular describes and include injection-technique modules, and the CPR certification must be current.
Treating continuing education as the only way to maintain competency. The circular calls it one way.
Treating counseling as optional because its topics are discretionary. Customary patient counseling must be provided before a dose is administered; only its content is left to judgment.
Placing the record-keeping duty on the individual pharmacist alone. The circular places it on the pharmacy where the eligible medication is administered.
Treating 24 hours as the deadline for every adverse event. A listed serious outcome, or an event requiring emergency medical services, must be reported immediately.

Assuming that telling the prescriber ends the matter. Where an improper dispensing results in serious injury or death, or a serious adverse drug event arises from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, 247 CMR 20.02 still requires a report to the Board. For any other dispensing error or serious adverse drug event, the circular's sentence still speaks of reporting to the Board, and the safe course is to make that report.

Settling who carries the Board report on one text alone. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) and (2) the pharmacy's Manager of Record files the report, and under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D the pharmacy informs the Department of Public Health of improper dispensing that results in serious injury or death and the manager of record reports a serious adverse drug event from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy. The circular, for its part, says the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board, in accordance with Board regulations. The texts do not say what that continuing responsibility consists of, so it is an error to treat the administering pharmacist or intern as the filer in the Manager of Record's place, and equally an error to treat that person as having no responsibility; the safe course is for that person to make sure the event reaches the Manager of Record at once and that the report to the Board is made in time.

Settling on one text alone which events the circular's Board-reporting sentence covers. 247 CMR 20.02(1) reaches improper dispensing only where it results in serious injury or death, and 247 CMR 20.02(2) reaches a serious adverse drug event only where it arises from a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, each on a seven-business-day period, so it is an error to treat every dispensing error or serious adverse drug event as one that 247 CMR 20.02 requires to be reported. But the circular's sentence, on its face, names every dispensing error and every serious adverse drug event, and the texts do not settle whether its words 'in accordance with Board regulations' narrow that set to the events 247 CMR 20.02 reaches or govern only how the report is made, so it is equally an error to conclude that an event outside 247 CMR 20.02 needs no report to the Board. The safe course is to bring the event to the Manager of Record at once and report it to the Board.
Confusing the administration record the circular strongly encourages sending to the prescriber with the adverse-event communication and reports it describes.
Assuming the privacy duty applies only at the injection. It runs at all times during the course of dispensing and administration.
Treating the administration notation as mandatory, a missing notation as invalidating the prescription, or contact with the prescriber as a precondition of administering.
Converting the circular's 'as soon after administration as practical' into a fixed or same-day deadline for sending the administration record.
Assuming a valid prescription opens methadone administration in a pharmacy that is not a registered opioid treatment program.

Assuming that a pharmacy could at least fill a methadone prescription written for maintenance or detoxification treatment. No paragraph of 21 CFR 1306.07 provides for prescribing a Schedule II narcotic drug for that purpose: paragraph (a) lets a practitioner separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program administer or dispense it directly, but not prescribe it, and paragraph (d), which includes prescribing, is confined to Schedule III, IV and V narcotic drugs.

Assuming the long-acting injectable buprenorphine or naltrexone and methadone travel the same pathway. The injectables are on the eligible list; methadone is addressed by the order-only route in a registered opioid treatment program.
Assuming a pharmacy intern may use the opioid treatment program route. The regulation and the circular's note name a pharmacist.
Assuming a listed medication must be administered whenever a patient asks. The circular states there is no requirement to administer.

Describing the pathway as a general licence to administer prescription injectables, or assuming a vaccine comes within it. It reaches an exhaustive list, and the list names no vaccine; vaccines rest on other authorities.

Treating the circular's eligible list as the whole of what a Massachusetts pharmacist or pharmacy intern may administer. The list closes the circular's prescription pathway; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) separately authorizes immunizations, 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(e) administration by order in an Opioid Treatment Program, and 105 CMR 700.003(F) vaccine administration under a Commissioner's order.

Carrying the circular's 18-or-older condition or its prescription instrument into immunization under 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), which reaches persons five years of age or older pursuant to the order of a practitioner.

Presenting the list, the route limit or the practice requirements as statute. The routes and their gates are statutory; the age limit, conditions and required contents of guidelines for mental health and substance use disorder drugs are regulatory; the list, the route limit, the practice requirements and the notation come from Department guidance.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Testosterone is listed in all salts as a gender-affirming care medication, and the statute's second pharmacist route is a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, so testosterone cypionate comes within the pathway on a prescription for that purpose and not on a prescription for another one.
Paliperidone palmitate is named among the long-acting injectable antipsychotics; because the list is by generic name, the brand under which it is supplied does not affect eligibility.

Buprenorphine is listed among the long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders, so an extended-release buprenorphine injection travels the ordinary prescription pathway, subject to the subcutaneous-or-intramuscular route limit, manufacturer approved labeling, any REMS requirements and the single-dose condition.

Naltrexone is listed among the long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders, so an extended-release naltrexone injection is eligible on a valid prescription for a person 18 years or older; eligibility does not oblige the pharmacist to administer it.
Methadone is not on the eligible list; a pharmacist may administer it for addiction treatment pursuant to an order, and only in a registered opioid treatment program.

Doxycycline is listed in the sexually transmitted infection category, with the entry extending to other medications to treat chlamydia; the listing does not relax the route limit, under which a pharmacist or pharmacy intern may only administer an eligible medication by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection.

authority.name: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124, Pharmacist Administration of Medications, March 11, 2026
authority.section: Dispensing by Administration, opening words and conditions (a) through (f); Prescriber Assessment

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 (March 11, 2026) provides that a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern may, without obtaining a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration (MCSR), dispense by administration (i.e. administer) FDA-approved drugs included in its list of Medications Eligible for Pharmacist or Pharmacy Intern Administration to persons 18 years or older, provided that: (a) the pharmacist or pharmacy intern is authorized to dispense controlled substances, in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112; (b) administration is conducted pursuant to a valid prescription; (c) administration is not intravenous; (d) the medication is available in single-dose packaging and prescribed in single doses, with or without refills; (e) the prescription is subject to reassessment by the prescriber at appropriate intervals, as determined by the prescriber, if applicable; and (f) the activity is conducted in accordance with Department guidelines. Under Prescriber Assessment, prescribers must regularly re-assess the patient and prescription at appropriate intervals, such as quarterly, to be determined by the prescriber; this assessment does not preclude the issuance of valid prescriptions with available refills; and if a pharmacist or pharmacy intern is presented with a prescription and has questions about the interval transpiring between assessments, routine communication with the prescriber is encouraged, but not required, prior to administration.
exceptions: Routine communication with the prescriber about the interval between assessments is encouraged, but not required, prior to administration.
Prescriber reassessment does not preclude the issuance of valid prescriptions with available refills.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 states that the following generic medications, which may have multiple brand names, are the only medications eligible to be administered by a pharmacist or pharmacy intern. Long-acting injectable antipsychotics: aripiprazole, aripiprazole lauroxil, fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate, risperidone and risperidone ER. Long-acting injectable medications for substance use disorders: buprenorphine and naltrexone. Gender-affirming care medications: testosterone (all salts). HIV prevention medications: cabotegravir, and lenacapavir (or other medications to prevent HIV). Sexually transmitted infection medications: ceftriaxone (IM injection), and doxycycline (or other medications to treat chlamydia). The circular states that there is no requirement for pharmacists or pharmacy interns to administer these medications, and that in accordance with 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) and this Department guidance pharmacists and pharmacy interns are authorized to administer certain medications for treating mental illness and substance use disorder, testosterone for gender-affirming care, antiviral therapy for prevention of HIV, and antibiotics for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections, citing M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9) itself reaches FDA approved mental health or substance use disorder treatment drugs, and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9)(d)1. requires the Department's guidelines to include requirements for the specific drugs permitted to be administered pursuant to 105 CMR 700.004(B)(9). The definition of Administer in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, clause (c)(ii) and (iii), separately reaches a registered pharmacist acting in accordance with a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, or a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or for the prevention of HIV.
exceptions: Two entries extend beyond a named generic medication: lenacapavir (or other medications to prevent HIV) and doxycycline (or other medications to treat chlamydia).
Testosterone is listed in all salts.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 provides that, to administer, a pharmacist or pharmacy intern must first receive training that is accredited by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Council on Pharmaceutical Education or a similar health authority or professional body appropriate for the medications being administered and their respective patient populations, and such training shall include learning modules on techniques for administration by injection. authority.name: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124, Pharmacist Administration of Medications, March 11, 2026
authority.section: Reporting Adverse Events; Administration – Medical Emergencies, second sentence

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 provides that any adverse events or reactions occurring as a result of a pharmacist or pharmacy intern administering a medication listed in the guidance should be appropriately communicated to the prescriber within 24 hours. If the adverse event includes one of the following outcomes, the event must be immediately reported to the prescriber: (i) death; (ii) a life-threatening outcome; (iii) inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization; (iv) additional treatment, testing, or monitoring in a hospital or emergency department; or (v) a persistent or significant incapacity or substantial disruption of the ability to conduct normal life functions. If the adverse event is the result of a dispensing error or is a serious adverse drug event, the pharmacist or pharmacy intern remains responsible for reporting the event to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, in accordance with Board regulations. Under Administration – Medical Emergencies, if emergency medical services are required, an adverse event must be immediately reported, as outlined in the circular's section on reporting adverse events.
exceptions: An adverse event with one of the five listed outcomes must be reported to the prescriber immediately rather than communicated within 24 hours.
An adverse event requiring emergency medical services must be reported immediately.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy reporting regulations
Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 20.02(1), a Manager of Record of a pharmacy shall report to the Board any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing. Under 247 CMR 20.02(2), a Manager of Record of a pharmacy shall report any serious adverse drug event that occurs as a result of a patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced, or compounded at the pharmacy, to: (a) the Board; (b) the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program; and (c) the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction; a Manager of Record shall report a serious adverse drug event within seven business days of the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b), a pharmacy shall inform the department of public health of any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, as defined by the department in regulations, as soon as is reasonably and practically possible, but not later than 7 business days after discovery of the improper dispensing. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(c), the manager of record of a pharmacy shall report any serious adverse drug event, as defined in section 51H of chapter 111, occurring as a result of the patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the manager of record's pharmacy, to the board, the federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman center for patient safety and medical error reduction, and this data shall be reported to the board within 7 business days of the knowledge of any serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee. On their terms, 247 CMR 20.02(1) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(b) reach improper dispensing only where it results in serious injury or death, and 247 CMR 20.02(2) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D(c) reach a serious adverse drug event only where it occurs as a result of a patient's interaction with a drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy.
exceptions: The reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies (247 CMR 20.02(5)).

authority.section: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6), read with the heading of 105 CMR 700.004(B)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 700.004(B), headed Exemptions from Requirement to Register, provides at paragraph (6) that a registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and pharmacy technician may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine, and other immunizations designated by the Department to persons five years of age or older provided that: (a) such registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern, or pharmacy technician is authorized to dispense controlled substances in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112 or Department guidance; (b) such administration is conducted pursuant to the order of a practitioner; (c) each pharmacy that provides immunizations shall follow Department guidelines to disclose whether it receives vaccines free of charge through the Massachusetts Immunization Program and shall notify patients that there may be a difference in cost between immunization services provided at a pharmacy and at a primary care provider's office; and (d) such activity is conducted in accordance with guidelines adopted by the Department which shall include, but not be limited to, requirements for: 1. training accredited by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Council on Pharmaceutical Education or a similar health authority or professional body; 2. pre-administration education and screening; 3. vaccine storage and handling; 4. administration of medication, including administration of controlled substances as necessary for the management of medical emergencies; 5. where immunization is being administered to a person younger than 18 years old, providing information on primary care providers in the pharmacy's geographic area; 6. if the purpose of the visit is for a childhood immunization other than the influenza vaccine, providing counseling on the importance of establishing and maintaining a relationship with a pediatric or family practice for ongoing medical and well-child care; 7. record keeping; and 8. reporting of adverse events.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Notwithstanding any other Department regulation, a health care professional duly licensed or certified by the Department, or a student duly enrolled in an approved programme acting within its policies, may possess and administer any vaccine designated by the Commissioner for prevention of a pandemic, novel or other vaccine-preventable disease, PROVIDED the Commissioner determines that there are or will be insufficient health care professionals available for timely administration AND issues an order authorizing it. Administration must accord with the Commissioner's order AND with the order or prescription of a duly registered practitioner authorized to issue one for a vaccine. A student may act only if authorised and supervised by a licensed and qualified health care professional.
exceptions: A student must be authorised and supervised by a licensed and qualified professional

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner may administer or dispense directly (but not prescribe) a narcotic drug in Schedule II to a narcotic dependent person for the purpose of maintenance or detoxification treatment if the practitioner is separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program and is in compliance with DEA regulations regarding treatment qualifications, security, records, and unsupervised use of the drugs pursuant to the Act. Under 1306.07(b) nothing in the section prohibits a practitioner who is not specifically registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program from dispensing (but not prescribing) narcotic drugs, in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws relating to controlled substances, to one person or for one person's use at one time for the purpose of initiating maintenance treatment or detoxification treatment (or both); not more than a three-day supply may be dispensed to the person or for the person's use at one time while arrangements are being made for referral for treatment, and such emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended. Under 1306.07(c) the section is not intended to impose any limitations on a physician or authorized hospital staff to administer or dispense narcotic drugs in a hospital to maintain or detoxify a person as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to administer or dispense narcotic drugs to persons with intractable pain in which no relief or cure is possible or none has been found after reasonable efforts. Under 1306.07(d) a practitioner may administer or dispense (including prescribe) any Schedule III, IV, or V narcotic drug for use in maintenance or detoxification treatment to a narcotic dependent person. Under 1306.07(f), notwithstanding the definition of dispense in 21 U.S.C. 802(10), a pharmacy may deliver a controlled substance to a practitioner, pursuant to a prescription that meets the requirements of 21 CFR 1306.04, for the purpose of administering the controlled substance by the practitioner if: it is delivered to the prescribing practitioner or the administering practitioner at the location listed on the practitioner's DEA certificate of registration; it is a narcotic drug in Schedule III, IV, or V to be administered for the purpose of maintenance or detoxification treatment by injection or implantation; the pharmacy, the prescribing practitioner and the administering practitioner are authorized to conduct those activities under the law of the State in which they take place; the prescription is not issued to supply any practitioner with a stock of controlled substances for the purpose of general dispensing to patients; it is to be administered only to the patient named on the prescription not later than 45 days after the date of receipt of the controlled substance by the practitioner; and the prescribing and administering practitioners, as applicable, maintain complete and accurate records of all controlled substances delivered, received, administered, or otherwise disposed of under paragraph (f), including the persons to whom the controlled substances were delivered.
exceptions: Paragraph (c): the section is not intended to impose any limitations on a physician or authorized hospital staff to administer or dispense narcotic drugs in a hospital to maintain or detoxify a person as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to administer or dispense narcotic drugs to persons with intractable pain in which no relief or cure is possible or none has been found after reasonable efforts.
